228:APA publishes high-quality research that undergoes a rigorous and ethical peer review process. Journal policies for authors are provided for transparency and clarity, including ethical expectations, AI guidance, and reuse.
230:The publication of a scientific article by an APA journal does not constitute its endorsement. The association will not condone any attempt to censor the reporting or discussion of science within its journals so long as it has been conducted ethically and meets the scientific standards of the profession. Further, the association will neither retract a published paper nor censure authors or editors for ethical scientific activities that yield potentially controversial findings. Scientific investigation is an evolving process: The ultimate evaluation of scientific results depends on a continuous exchange of ideas and reexamination of ideas and findings.
234:APA policy prohibits an author from submitting the same manuscript for concurrent consideration by two or more publications. See also APA Journals® Internet Posting Guidelines.
235:APA requires authors to reveal any possible conflict of interest in the conduct and reporting of research (e.g., financial interests in a test or procedure, funding by pharmaceutical companies for drug research). Download the Disclosure of Interests Form (PDF, 38KB)opens in new window.
238: Author contributorship and responsibilities of authors
239:⁠APA follows a contributorship rather than an authorship model, meaning that authors are not only those who do the writing but also those who have made substantial scientific contributions to a study. 
241:Authorship is reserved for persons who make a substantial contribution to and who accept responsibility for a published work. Individuals should take authorship credit only for work they have performed or to which they have substantially contributed (APA Ethics Code Standard 8.12a, Publication Credit). Authorship encompasses, therefore, not only those who do the writing but also those who have made substantial scientific contributions to a study. Substantial professional contributions may include formulating the problem or hypothesis, structuring the experimental design, organizing and conducting the statistical analysis, or interpreting the results and findings. Those who so contribute are listed in the byline. Lesser contributions, which do not constitute authorship, may be acknowledged in the author note (see Section 2.7; see also a taxonomy of authorship in the natural sciences called at CRediT). Lesser contributions may include such supportive functions as designing or building the apparatus, suggesting or advising about the analysis, collecting or entering the data, modifying or structuring a computer program, recruiting participants, and obtaining animals. Conducting routine observations or diagnoses for use in studies does not constitute authorship. Combinations of these (and other) tasks, however, may justify authorship.
242:Some APA journals have adopted the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT)opens in new window to automate author contributions statements in their published articles. CRediT is a high-level taxonomy comprised of 14 roles that describe each author’s specific contribution(s) to the scholarly output. Authors can select more than one contributor role, and the same role can be attributed to more than one person.
245:Each author is expected to have made substantial contributions to the conception or design of the work; or the acquisition, analysis, or interpretation of data; or the creation of new software used in the work; or have drafted the work or substantively revised it; AND to have approved the submitted version (and any substantially modified version that involves the author’s contribution to the study); AND to have agreed both to be personally accountable for the author’s own contributions and to ensure that questions related to the accuracy or integrity of any part of the work, even ones in which the author was not personally involved, are appropriately investigated, resolved, and the resolution documented in the literature.
246:*McNutt, M.K., Bradford, M., Drazen, J. M., Hanson, B., Howard, B., Hall Jamieson, K., Kiermer, V., Marcus, E., Kline Pope, B., Schekman, R., Swaminathan, S., Stang, P. J., Verma, I. M. (2018). Transparency in authors’ contributions and responsibilities to promote integrity in scientific publication. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115, 2557-2560. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1715374115opens in new window.
253:A request for possible correction may be made by the author(s), editor, readers, or the institution where the research took place. Requests go to the journal's current editor or APA staff.
254:- Once the editor is alerted, they confer with APA staff and the author(s) on whether the edit rises to the level of a formal correction notice.
255:- If the edit does warrant a correction notice, the editor will inform the author(s) of the need for a correction notice and the author(s) will work with APA staff to create it.
256:- Once the correction notice is finalized with the author(s) and reviewed by the editor, APA Staff will have the correction notice published online and in print.
264:Authors are encouraged to bring errors to editors' attention, especially when they affect the validity of study finding. Situations warranting retraction include those in which an article was plagiarized; its findings were previously published elsewhere without justification; if its findings are unreliable, either as a result of error (e.g., miscalculation or experimental error) or as a result of misconduct (e.g., fabrication of data or falsification via image manipulation); or that report unethical research as defined by the APA ethical guidelines or an institutional review board. For these instances, the article is marked as retracted from the journal.
266:A request for a possible retraction may be made by the author(s), editor, readers, or the institution where the research took place. Requests go to journal's current editor or APA staff.  
267:- Once the editor is alerted, they will confer with the APA publisher, the chief editorial advisor, and the author(s) on whether the edits rise to the level of a formal retraction notice.
268:- If it is found that the edits warrant a retraction notice, the editor and author(s) will work with APA staff to create the retraction notice.
269:- Once the retraction notice is finalized with the editor and author(s), APA staff will have the retraction notice published online and in print.
271: Policy on author name changes after publication
272:APA will change authors’ names in the digital record on request. Respecting authors’ autonomy and recognizing that authors’ names may change after articles have been published, APA Publishing will update author names without publishing an accompanying correction notice. Changes will be made to the digital record for APA-published ebooks or journal articles that have already appeared in print.
273:This policy was suggested by APA Division 44opens in new window (Society for the Psychology of Sexual Orientation and Gender Diversity) and formally recommended by the Publications and Communications Board in May 2020. The P&C Board recognizes that transgender and nonbinary authors are often subjected to gatekeeping discrimination when updating their records and has extended the option to all requesting authors, regardless of their reason for the change. 
274:Authors who change their name and wish to update their published articles or ebooks may request corrections via emailopens in new window. For articles published before this policy was posted in August 2020, coauthors will be notified of the change so that they can update their publication records.
275: APA policy on the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in scholarly materials
276:For this policy, AI refers to generative LLM AI tools and does not include grammar-checking software, citation software, or plagiarism detectors.
277:- When a generative artificial intelligence (AI) model is used in the drafting of a manuscript for an APA publication, the use of AI must be disclosed in the manuscript and cited. For examples, see disclosure guidance.
278:- AI cannot be named as an author on an APA scholarly publication.
279:- The authors are responsible for the accuracy of any information in their article. Authors must verify any information and citations provided to them by an AI tool. Authors may use but must disclose AI tools for specific purposes such as editing.
280:- No submitted content may be entered into generative AI tools as this violates the confidentiality of the process.
282:- APA Journals policy on generative AI: Additional guidance
283:- APA Style Blog: Citing generative AI in APA Style: Part 1—Reference formats
284:- COPE Position Statement: Authorship and AI tools | COPE: Committee on Publication Ethicsopens in new window
285:- US Copyright Office Guidance: Federal Register :: Copyright Registration Guidance: Works Containing Material Generated by Artificial Intelligenceopens in new window
287:The seventh edition of APA’s Publication Manualopens in new window instructs authors to provide funder and conflict-of-interest information in the author note. Authors should disclose even interests that could potentially be perceived as conflicts. 
288:To add a further layer of transparency, many editors ask authors to provide a statement attesting that there is no potential perceived conflict of interest.
290:Authors are to avoid plagiarism and duplicate or fragmented publication. Duplicate publication involves publishing the same data more than once. Fragmented (or piecemeal) publication involves dividing the report of a research project into multiple articles. Duplicate or fragmented publications are misleading if they appear to represent independent instances. They can distort the scientific literature, especially in reviews or meta-analyses.
291:Sometimes authors want to publish essentially the same material in different journals in order to reach different audiences. If you think that such duplicate publication is justified, the article must include reference to the original report—both to inform editors, reviewers, and readers and as a necessary fulfillment of the author’s obligations to the previous copyright holder.
292:In general, the author should inform the editor about the existence of other reports from the same research project at the time of submission.
294:In light of changing patterns of scientific knowledge dissemination, APA requires authors to provide information on prior dissemination of the data and narrative interpretations of the data/research appearing in the manuscript (e.g., if some or all were presented at a conference or meeting, posted on a listserv, shared on a website, including academic social networks like ResearchGate, etc.). This information (2–4 sentences) must be provided as part of the author note. 
297:APA expects authors to adhere to these standards. Specifically, APA expects authors to have their data available throughout the editorial review process and for at least 5 years after the date of publication. Many APA journals adhere to Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) Guidelinesopens in new window, and authors should refer to each journal for its data-sharing policy.
299:Authors who have posted their manuscripts to preprint archives, such as PsyArXiv, prior to submission should include a link to the preprint in the author note.
300:Authors of articles published in APA journals—the authoritative document, i.e., peer-reviewed publication of record—may post a prepublication copy of the final manuscript, as accepted for publication as a word processing file, on their personal website; their employer’s server; their institution's repository; a preprint repository like APA’s designated preprint server, PsyArXiv; reference managers (e.g., Mendeley); and author social networks (e.g., Academia.edu and ResearchGate) after it is accepted for publication.
302:Author Resource Center

APA policy on the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in scholarly materials
For this policy, AI refers to generative LLM AI tools and does not include grammar-checking software, citation software, or plagiarism detectors.
- When a generative artificial intelligence (AI) model is used in the drafting of a manuscript for an APA publication, the use of AI must be disclosed in the manuscript and cited. For examples, see disclosure guidance.
- AI cannot be named as an author on an APA scholarly publication.
- The authors are responsible for the accuracy of any information in their article. Authors must verify any information and citations provided to them by an AI tool. Authors may use but must disclose AI tools for specific purposes such as editing.
- No submitted content may be entered into generative AI tools as this violates the confidentiality of the process.
Additional reading material:
- APA Journals policy on generative AI: Additional guidance

2: APA Journals policy on generative AI: Additional guidance
107: Authors, Editors, and Reviewers
227:APA Journals policy on generative AI 
229:Generative artificial intelligence, specifically the kind based on Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, has become a transformative force in many fields. Scholarly writing and publishing are no different, and generative AI has begun to have an impact on scholarly work.
230:In response to this impact, the APA Publications and Communications Board has approved policies regarding the use of generative AI in scholarly materials. These policies (as well as APA policies on other potential issues in scholarly publishing, and additional reading on the subject) can be found on the APA Publishing Policies page and will continue to develop as we gain a better understanding of the effects of generative AI on scholarly publishing.
231:APA’s current policies on generative AI are:
232:- When a generative AI model is used in the drafting of a manuscript for an APA publication, the use of AI must be disclosed in the methods section and cited.
233:- AI cannot be named as an author on an APA scholarly publication.
234:Authors
235:APA policy states that authors are responsible for the accuracy of any information in their article. This means that authors must verify any information and citations provided to them by an AI tool. Authors may use, but must disclose, AI tools for specific purposes such as editing.
236:For guidance about when and where to disclose the use of a Generative AI tool, please see the disclosure guidance section below.
237:Additionally, please note that when information is entered into generative AI, the organization which runs the generative AI will likely have access to this data. Authors should be aware of this possibility and how it may impact the privacy of participants in their studies, as well as how it may impact their own privacy and intellectual property. For this reason, journal editors and reviewers may not enter materials from submitted manuscripts into generative AI as it would constitute a violation of the confidentiality of the peer review process.
238:Disclosure guidance
239:Guiding principles for authors and editors about what output to disclose from generative AI tools:
240:- Authors need to be transparent, providing the necessary information for readers to understand how generative artificial intelligence (AI) was used during the research and manuscript drafting process. Disclose the use in the most relevant place in the manuscript, most likely the Introduction or Method sections.
241:- Authors need to maintain ethical approaches to using generative AI, including not entering confidential material into open generative AI tools, for example, research data or client notes that may make a participant/client identifiable.
242:- Authors need to take responsibility for the information provided by generative AI tools, including verifying the information received via generative AI searches by reading original sources used in AI output.
243:- Authors need to provide attribution to the generative AI tool in cases where the tool was used to generate ideas, content, analysis, code, or research elements. If you would provide attribution to a human contributor, you should most likely provide attribution to a generative AI tool for a similar activity. 
244:Authors should consider the disclosure of AI in the context of existing resources such as the Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association (7th ed.), the Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct, the Contributor Role Taxonomy (CRediTopens in new window), and guidance provided by the institution that approved the author’s research. For curated AI topics, consult the APA Style website and blog.
245:Noncomprehensive examples of these principles are provided next to aid authors and editors in thinking about what needs to be disclosed when using generative AI. Some examples recommend that authors preserve the output of generative AI in their private records in case it is requested during peer review or after publication. Researchers should document for their own records the prompts used with AI tools. To the extent that it helps readers, these prompts can be included where the AI use is disclosed, or elsewhere as appropriate, such as an appendix.

118:Access fees may apply
228:The APA Journals Office supports authors’ choices on how to publish their work. We are committed to offering options that we believe comply with most funder and institutional requirements and support both self-archiving (“green”) and APC (paid for via an article processing charge and also known as “gold”) Open Access options. Submitting a manuscript for peer review is free of charge.
235: Open Access Agreements
237:All APA authors, including those without APC funding, have the option of self-archiving (also known as “green” open access), outlined in our internet posting guidelines.
241:Please indicate your funder source at the manuscript submission stage. Authors whose funders require self-archiving under a CC-BY license (PDF, 106KB)opens in new window may do so. Note for authors who have received funding from NIH and other U.S. government agencies: as a service to authors who have received funding from the U.S. government, we will handle deposit of the accepted manuscript to PubMed after acceptance with author consent. We aim to do this by the time of the publication of the version of record, but authors have the option to self-deposit instead.
242:Note that we comply fully with the open access requirements of UKRI, Wellcome Trust, and NIHR. Where required by their funder, authors retain the right to distribute their author accepted manuscript (AAM), such as via an institutional and/or subject repository (e.g. EuropePMC), under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license for release no later than the date of first online publication.
244:Choose one of our article processing charge (APC) Open Access options to make your article freely available immediately on publication.
245:Open Access in APA’s Hybrid Journals
246:APC Open Access is offered for all APA subscription-based journals. Authors can make their article freely available for an article processing charge (APC) of $3,500 USD.
247:APC Open Access articles are published under a CC-BY-NC-NDopens in new window (Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial-No Derivatives) license, allowing others to download and share them for noncommercial and non-derivative use as long as authors are credited. As such, all requests for APC Open Access must be submitted BEFORE publication. APA will not grant post-publication requests to make articles open access.
251: is APA’s open access, interdisciplinary, peer-reviewed journal publishing original work in the area of human–technology interaction with a focus on human behavior at the individual or group level. Authors make their articles freely available in this journal for an article processing charge (APC) of $1,800 USD.
252:Articles are published under a CC-BY-NC-NDopens in new window (Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial-No Derivatives) license, allowing others to download and share them for noncommercial use as long as authors are credited. Authors whose funders require it may publish under a CC-BY license (PDF, 107KB)opens in new window.
254:Open Access Agreements
255:Authors affiliated with institutions participating in APA’s open access agreements (also known as “Read and Publish” agreements) have the option to publish open access in all hybrid APA journals at no cost to the authors.
256:The aim of the agreements is to bolster both research access and open access publishing and to provide authors with a simplified process to comply with funder mandates at no direct cost to authors.

233: Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) Guidelines
234:In support of rigorous, transparent research, a growing number of APA journals now include Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) Guidelines in their manuscript submission instructions. In 2020, APA became one of more than 5,000 signatories of the TOP Guidelines developed by the Center for Open Science.
235:The TOP Guidelines cover eight fundamental aspects of research planning and reporting that can be followed by journals and authors at three levels of adherence. From lower to higher levels of adherence, they are: disclosure (Level 1), requirement (Level 2), and verification (Level 3).
236:Inclusion of the TOP Guidelines in APA journals is an exciting step for open science in psychology. The practices described by the guidelines offer many benefits not only to authors but to psychological science. Transparency encourages greater collaboration among researchers, facilitates replication of certain types of studies, and promotes more rigorous science.
237:Check out our TOP announcement to learn more about the guidelines and details on participating APA journals. You can also find detailed guidance on the open science tab of each journal’s webpage, as well as in the submission guidelines. As of fall 2023, authors are required to disclose TOP compliance only in the Methods section of their manuscript. Read our interview with APA journal editor Panayiota Kendeou, PhD to learn how the TOP Guidelines have been implemented at the Journal of Educational Psychology and understand how TOP can impact authors who wish to publish in a journal.
239:Preregistration of original research, clinical trials, and meta-analyses can help increase transparency. APA’s Publication Manual (7th edition) asks authors to provide registration details in the author note, and journals that have adopted the TOP guidelines will also ask for information to be reported in the study’s method section.
254:Many APA journals have adopted the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT)opens in new window to automate author contributions statements in their published articles. CRediT is a high-level taxonomy comprised of 14 roles that describe each author’s specific contribution(s) to a given piece of scholarly output. Authors can select more than one contributor role, and the same role can be attributed to more than one person.

 Author contribution statements using CRediT
Authors who include author contribution statements in the author note of a manuscript promote accuracy, transparency, and visibility for the range of contributions to the published work. APA authors are encouraged to include author contribution statements in the author notes of their manuscripts.
APA journals follow a contributorship rather than an authorship model, meaning that authors are not only those who do the writing but also those who have made substantial scientific contributions to a study (see Standard 8.12a of the APA Ethics Code and the Publication Manual, 7th ed. for more information on what contributions constitute authorship).
Many APA journals have adopted the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT)opens in new window to automate author contributions statements in their published articles. CRediT is a high-level taxonomy comprised of 14 roles that describe each author’s specific contribution(s) to a given piece of scholarly output. Authors can select more than one contributor role, and the same role can be attributed to more than one person. 
This taxonomy allows for a broader and more representative acknowledgment of the work of researchers who may otherwise not be represented or credited.
The use of CRediT likewise presents the opportunity to mitigate author disputes because contributor roles are identified and clearly reported from the beginning stages of manuscript review.
CRediT roles are tagged with metadata, which means that author contributions are both visible and trackable.
For APA journals that have adopted CRediT, authors are required to identify each author’s contribution(s) to the manuscript as part of the manuscript submission data in Editorial Manager. When an article is accepted, the contributor roles are published as part of the author note.
All core APA Journals are required to publish author contribution statements using CRediT. The following journals currently publish author contribution statements using CRediT:

_Decision_ is a multidisciplinary journal focused on scientific research into human judgment and decision-making. This includes research on neural, cognitive, social, economic, cultural, and environmental aspects of people’s decisions.

_Decision_ publishes articles on all areas related to the psychology of judgment and decision-making including probabilistic inference, prediction, evaluation, choice, decisions under risk or uncertainty, and economic games. The journal publishes articles reporting new empirical research that adds to our understanding of judgment and decision making, and articles that present and evaluate new theory.

To achieve this goal, _Decision_ publishes three types of articles: long articles that make major theoretical contributions, shorter articles that make valuable empirical contributions addressing important research questions, and brief review articles that target current theoretical trends or new topics in decision making. The journal generally favors articles that include large-scale confirmatory tests of theory, or that report multiple studies which, together, address a substantive research question. Articles reporting laboratory research or field experiments are welcome, as are those which include replication studies addressing key theoretical or empirical issues.

Markdown Content:

1	Title: Decision Submission Guidelines
2	
3	URL Source: https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/dec/submit
4	
5	Markdown Content:
6	**Prior to submission, please carefully read and follow all submission guidelines.** Manuscripts that do not conform to the submission guidelines may be returned without review.
7	
8	To submit to the editorial office of Tim Rakow, PhD, please submit manuscripts electronically through the Manuscript Submission Portal, in Microsoft Word (.docx) or LaTex (.tex) as a zip file with an accompanied Portable Document Format (.pdf) of a manuscript file.
9	
10	Prepare manuscripts according to the _Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association_ using the 7 th edition. Manuscripts may be copyedited for bias-free language (see Chapter 5 of the _Publication Manual_). [APA Style and Grammar Guidelines](https://apastyle.apa.org/style-grammar-guidelines?utm_source=apa.org&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=/pubs/journals/dec/submit&utm_term=body) for the 7 th edition are available.
11	
12	[Submit Manuscript opens in new window](https://www.editorialmanager.com/dec/default1.aspx)
13	
14	Tim Rakow   
15	_King's College London_  
16	[Email opens in new window](mailto:[email redacted])
17	
18	## Manuscript types
19	
20	_Decision_ will publish three types of articles. All page limits are exclusive of tables, figures, and references:
21	
22	*   full length articles (35 pages) that make major theoretical contributions
23	*   shorter articles (15 pages) that make major empirical contributions addressing important theoretical issues
24	*   brief review articles (15 pages) that target rapidly rising theoretical trends or new theoretical topics in decision making
25	
26	## Masked/Unmasked review
27	
28	Upon selecting an article type, authors can also choose between masked or unmasked review (i.e., “Unmasked article” or “Article with Masked review requested”).
29	
30	## Equity, diversity, and inclusion in _Decision_
31	
32	_Decision_ is committed to improving equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI) in scientific research, in line with the [APA Publishing EDI framework](https://www.apa.org/pubs/authors/equity-diversity-inclusion) and APA’s [trio of 2021 resolutions](https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2021/10/apology-systemic-racism) to address systemic racism in psychology.
33	
34	The journal encourages submissions which extend beyond Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic (WEIRD) samples ([Henrich, et al., 2010 opens in new window](https://doi.org/10.1038/466029a)), and study designs that address heterogeneity within diverse samples.   
35	To promote a more equitable research and publication process, _Decision_ has adopted the following standards for inclusive research reporting.
36	
37	### Participant description, sample justification, and informed consent
38	
39	Authors are encouraged to include a detailed description of the study participants in the method section of each empirical report, including (but not limited to) age, sex, gender, and any other demographic information potentially relevant to the paper.
40	
41	In both the abstract and in the discussion section of the manuscript, authors are encouraged to discuss the diversity of their study samples and the generalizability of their findings (see also the constraints on generality section below).
42	
43	The method section also must include a statement describing how informed consent was obtained from the participants (or their parents/guardians), including for secondary use of data if applicable, and indicate that the study was conducted in compliance with an appropriate Internal Review Board.
44	
45	### Constraints on generality
46	
47	In a subsection of the discussion titled "Constraints on generality," authors should include a detailed discussion of the limits on generality (see [Simons, Shoda, & Lindsay, 2017 opens in new window](https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691617708630)). In this section, authors should detail grounds for concluding why the results are may or may not be specific to the characteristics of the participants. They should address limits on generality not only for participants but for materials, procedures, and context. Authors should also specify which methods they think could be varied without affecting the result and which should remain constant.
48	
49	### Openness and transparency
50	
51	_Decision_ encourages both methodological and data transparency to ensure the reproducibility of research results. Thus, we ask authors to ensure their manuscripts meet certain standards aligned with the open science movement.
52	
53	### Data, materials, and code
54	
55	Authors must state whether data and study materials are available and, if so, where to access them. Recommended repositories include [APA’s repository](https://osf.io/meetings/apa%20target=) on the Open Science Framework (OSF), or authors can access a full [list of other recommended repositories opens in new window](https://re3data.org/).
56	
57	In both the author note and at the end of the method section, specify whether and where the data and material will be available or note the legal or ethical reasons for not doing so. For submissions with quantitative or simulation analytic methods, state whether the study analysis code is available, and, if so, where to access it (or the legal or ethical reason why it is not available).
58	
59	For example:
60	
61	*   All data have been made publicly available at the [repository name] and can be accessed at [persistent URL or DOI].
62	*   Materials and analysis code for this study are not available.
63	*   The code behind this analysis/simulation has been made publicly available at the [repository name] and can be accessed at [persistent URL or DOI].
64	
65	The APA Publication Manual ([7th ed.opens in new window](https://doi.org/10.1037/0000165-000)) stipulates that "authorship encompasses…not only persons who do the writing but also those who have made substantial scientific contributions to a study." In the spirit of transparency and openness, this journal has adopted the [Contributor Roles Taxonomy opens in new window](https://credit.niso.org/) (CRediT) to describe each author's individual contributions to the work. CRediT offers authors the opportunity to share an accurate and detailed description of their diverse contributions to a manuscript.
66	
67	Submitting authors will be prompted to select one or more contributor roles for each author at initial submission. All authors should have reviewed and agreed to their individual contribution(s) before submission. If the manuscript is accepted for publication, an Author Contributions Statement will be generated during the typesetting process and published in the author note of the final article. It is not necessary for authors to provide a written Author Contributions Statement upon submission.
68	
69	CRediT includes 14 contributor roles, as described below:
70	
71	*   **Conceptualization:**Ideas; formulation or evolution of overarching research goals and aims.
72	*   **Data curation:**Management activities to annotate (produce metadata), scrub data and maintain research data (including software code, where it is necessary for interpreting the data itself) for initial use and later reuse.
73	*   **Formal analysis:**Application of statistical, mathematical, computational, or other formal techniques to analyze or synthesize study data.
74	*   **Funding acquisition:**Acquisition of the financial support for the project leading to this publication.
75	*   **Investigation:**Conducting a research and investigation process, specifically performing the experiments, or data/evidence collection.
76	*   **Methodology:**Development or design of methodology; creation of models.
77	*   **Project administration:**Management and coordination responsibility for the research activity planning and execution.
78	*   **Resources:**Provision of study materials, reagents, materials, patients, laboratory samples, animals, instrumentation, computing resources, or other analysis tools.
79	*   **Software:**Programming, software development; designing computer programs; implementation of the computer code and supporting algorithms; testing of existing code components.
80	*   **Supervision:**Oversight and leadership responsibility for the research activity planning and execution, including mentorship external to the core team.
81	*   **Validation:**Verification, whether as a part of the activity or separate, of the overall replication/reproducibility of results/experiments and other research outputs.
82	*   **Visualization:**Preparation, creation and/or presentation of the published work, specifically visualization/data presentation.
83	*   **Writing—original draft:**Preparation, creation and/or presentation of the published work, specifically writing the initial draft (including substantive translation).
84	*   **Writing—review and editing:**Preparation, creation and/or presentation of the published work by those from the original research group, specifically critical review, commentary or revision—including pre- or post-publication stages.
85	
86	Authors can claim credit for more than one contributor role, and the same role can be attributed to more than one author. Not all roles will be applicable to any particular scholarly work.
87	
88	## Registered Reports
89	
90	The journal also invites submission of Registered Reports. Registered Reports require a two-stage review process.
91	
92	Stage 1 is the submission of the registration, so-called Stage 1 manuscript. This is a partial manuscript that includes introduction, theoretical framework, rationale for the study, hypotheses, experimental design, and methods (including an analysis plan). The partial manuscript will be reviewed for significance, theoretical framework, methodological approach, and analysis plan.
93	
94	If the Stage 1 Registered Report manuscript receives an “in-principal acceptance (IPA)” it means that the study has the potential to be published if it is performed exactly as proposed (also including the proposed statistical evaluation) regardless of the outcome of the study. After this stage and before data collection begins the study is pre-registered (e.g., through the Registered Report tools from OSF).
95	
96	In Stage 2, the full paper undergoes a second peer-review process, checking if the study protocol was implemented and if the reasons for potential changes were acceptable. Nevertheless, a rejection is still possible, namely if the study’s execution and analysis diverged too much from the proposed study design and/or the manuscript is low quality. The refinement of the discussion and conclusions may still require further revision, but the process will be expedited.
97	
98	## Registered Adversarial Collaborations
99	
100	The journal also invites submission of Registered Adversarial Collaborations. These are a sub-type of Registered Reports in which two researchers (or research teams) with different positions on a scientific matter agree to collaborate on the design, data collection, analysis, and reporting of jointly-conducted research. The purpose of this research is to provide some resolution on the point(s) of difference. The rationale for adversarial collaboration is that this will often be a more constructive approach to resolving scientific disputes than researchers pursuing independent lines of research. To this end, the researchers may propose multiple studies for their Registered Adversarial Collaboration (e.g., studies having different methodologies, studies each addressing a separate point of difference).
101	
102	Registered Adversarial Collaborations also require a two-stage review process.
103	
104	Stage 1 is the same as for a standard Registered Report, except that:
105	
106	1.   The partial manuscript includes details of the competing theoretical positions of the researchers and is explicit on how the study methods allow for resolution on the point(s) of difference.
107	2.   The researchers submit a Writing Plan that outlines the plan for producing the final manuscript (e.g., whether an independent ‘referee’ will oversee the writing, what proportion of the Discussion is given over to interpretations of the data that are written jointly or independently by the two researchers).
108	
109	Stage 2 is the same as for a standard Registered Report.
110	
111	## Manuscript preparation
112	
113	### Formatting
114	
115	Double-space all copy. Other formatting instructions, as well as instructions on preparing tables, figures, references, metrics, and abstracts, appear in the _Manual_. Additional guidance on APA Style is available on the [APA Style website opens in new window](https://www.apastyle.apa.org/).
116	
117	Below are additional instructions regarding the preparation of display equations, computer code, and tables.
118	
119	### Display equations
120	
121	We strongly encourage you to use MathType (third-party software) or Equation Editor 3.0 (built into pre-2007 versions of Word) to construct your equations, rather than the equation support that is built into Word 2007 and Word 2010. Equations composed with the built-in Word 2007/Word 2010 equation support are converted to low-resolution graphics when they enter the production process and must be rekeyed by the typesetter, which may introduce errors.
122	
123	To construct your equations with MathType or Equation Editor 3.0:
124	
125	*   Go to the Text section of the Insert tab and select Object.
126	*   Select MathType or Equation Editor 3.0 in the drop-down menu.
127	
128	If you have an equation that has already been produced using Microsoft Word 2007 or 2010 and you have access to the full version of MathType 6.5 or later, you can convert this equation to MathType by clicking on MathType Insert Equation. Copy the equation from Microsoft Word and paste it into the MathType box. Verify that your equation is correct, click File, and then click Update. Your equation has now been inserted into your Word file as a MathType Equation.
129	
130	Use Equation Editor 3.0 or MathType only for equations or for formulas that cannot be produced as Word text using the Times or Symbol font.
131	
132	### Computer code
133	
134	Because altering computer code in any way (e.g., indents, line spacing, line breaks, page breaks) during the typesetting process could alter its meaning, we treat computer code differently from the rest of your article in our production process. To that end, we request separate files for computer code.
135	
136	### In the text of the article
137	
138	If you would like to include code in the text of your published manuscript, please submit a separate file with your code exactly as you want it to appear, using Courier New font with a type size of 8 points. We will make an image of each segment of code in your article that exceeds 40 characters in length. (Shorter snippets of code that appear in text will be typeset in Courier New and run in with the rest of the text.) If an appendix contains a mix of code and explanatory text, please submit a file that contains the entire appendix, with the code keyed in 8-point Courier New.
139	
140	### Tables
141	
142	Use Word's insert table function when you create tables. Using spaces or tabs in your table will create problems when the table is typeset and may result in errors.
143	
144	### LaTex files
145	
146	LaTex files (.tex) should be uploaded with all other files such as BibTeX Generated Bibliography File (.bbl) or Bibliography Document (.bib) together in a compressed ZIP file folder for the manuscript submission process. In addition, a Portable Document Format (.pdf) of the manuscript file must be uploaded for the peer-review process.
147	
148	## Academic writing and English language editing services
149	
150	Authors who feel that their manuscript may benefit from additional academic writing or language editing support prior to submission are encouraged to seek out such services at their host institutions, engage with colleagues and subject matter experts, and/or consider several vendors that offer discounts to APA authors.
151	
152	Please note that APA does not endorse or take responsibility for the service providers listed. It is strictly a referral service. Use of such service is not mandatory for publication in an APA journal. Use of one or more of these services does not guarantee selection for peer review, manuscript acceptance, or preference for publication in any APA journal.
153	
154	APA can place supplemental materials online, available via the published article in the APA PsycArticles® database.
155	
156	## Abstract and keywords
157	
158	All manuscripts must include an abstract containing a maximum of 250 words typed on a separate page. After the abstract, please supply up to five keywords or brief phrases.
159	
160	## References
161	
162	List references in alphabetical order. Each listed reference should be cited in text, and each text citation should be listed in the references section.
163	
164	Examples of basic reference formats:
165	
166	**Journal article**
167	
168	McCauley, S. M., & Christiansen, M. H. (2019). Language learning as language use: A cross-linguistic model of child language development. Psychological Review, 126(1), 1–51. [https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000126 opens in new window](https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000126)
169	
170	**Authored book**
171	
172	Brown, L. S. (2018). Feminist therapy (2nd ed.). American Psychological Association. [https://doi.org/10.1037/0000092-000 opens in new window](https://doi.org/10.1037/0000092-000)
173	
174	**Chapter in an edited book**
175	
176	Balsam, K. F., Martell, C. R., Jones. K. P., Safren, S. A. (2019). Affirmative cognitive behavior therapy with sexual and gender minority people. In G. Y. Iwamasa & P. A. Hays (Eds.), Culturally responsive cognitive behavior therapy: Practice and supervision (2nd ed., pp. 287–314). American Psychological Association. [https://doi.org/10.1037/0000119-012 opens in new window](https://doi.org/10.1037/0000119-012)
177	
178	**Data set citation**
179	
180	Alegria, M., Jackson, J. S., Kessler, R. C., & Takeuchi, D. (2016). Collaborative Psychiatric Epidemiology Surveys (CPES), 2001–2003 [Data set]. Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research.[https://doi.org/10.3886/ICPSR20240.v8 opens in new window](https://doi.org/10.3886/ICPSR20240.v8)
181	
182	**Software/Code citation**
183	
184	Viechtbauer, W. (2010). Conducting meta-analyses in R with the metafor package.Journal of Statistical Software, 36(3), 1–48.[https://www.jstatsoft.org/v36/i03/opens in new window](https://www.jstatsoft.org/v36/i03/)
185	
186	Wickham, H. et al.,(2019). Welcome to the tidyverse. Journal of Open Source Software, 4(43), 1686,[https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.01686 opens in new window](https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.01686)
187	
188	All data, program code, and other methods must be appropriately cited in the text and listed in the references section.
189	
190	## Tables and figures
191	
192	### Tables
193	
194	Tables should adhere to[APA Style opens in new window](https://apastyle.apa.org/style-grammar-guidelines?utm_source=apa.org&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=/pubs/journals/dec/submit&utm_term=body). Use Word’s Insert Table function to create tables, and do not insert tabs or extra spaces to align columns as this will create problems when the table is typeset.
195	
196	### Figures
197	
198	Preferred formats for graphics files are TIFF and JPG, and preferred format for vector-based files is EPS. Graphics downloaded or saved from web pages are not acceptable for publication.Multipanel figures (i.e., figures with parts labeled a, b, c, d, etc.) should be assembled into one file. When possible, please place symbol legends below the figure instead of to the side.
199	
200	#### Resolution
201	
202	*   All color line art and halftones: 300 DPI
203	*   Black and white line tone and gray halftone images: 600 DPI
204	
205	#### Line weights
206	
207	*   Adobe Photoshop images
208	*   Color (RGB, CMYK) images: 2 pixels
209	*   Grayscale images: 4 pixels
210	*   Adobe Illustrator Images
211	*   Stroke weight: 0.5 points
212	
213	APA offers authors the option to publish their figures online in color without the costs associated with print publication of color figures.
214	
215	The same caption will appear on both the online (color) and print (black and white) versions. To ensure that the figure can be understood in both formats, authors should add alternative wording (e.g., “the red (dark gray) bars represent”) as needed.
216	
217	#### Color figure fees
218	
219	For authors who prefer their figures to be published in color both in print and online, original color figures can be printed in color at the editor's and publisher's discretion provided the author agrees to pay:
220	
221	*   $900 for one figure
222	*   An additional$600 for the second figure
223	*   An additional$450 for each subsequent figure
224	
225	### Display equations
226	
227	We strongly encourage you to use MathType (third-party software) or Equation Editor 3.0 (built into pre-2007 versions of Word) to construct your equations, rather than the equation support that is built into Word 2007 and Word 2010. Equations composed with the built-in Word 2007/Word 2010 equation support are converted to low-resolution graphics when they enter the production process and must be rekeyed by the typesetter, which may introduce errors.
228	
229	To construct your equations with MathType or Equation Editor 3.0:
230	
231	*   Go to the Text section of the Insert tab and select Object.
232	*   Select MathType or Equation Editor 3.0 in the drop-down menu.
233	
234	If you have an equation that has already been produced using Microsoft Word 2007 or 2010 and you have access to the full version of MathType 6.5 or later, you can convert this equation to MathType by clicking on MathType Insert Equation. Copy the equation from Microsoft Word and paste it into the MathType box. Verify that your equation is correct, click File, and then click Update. Your equation has now been inserted into your Word file as a MathType Equation.
235	
236	Use Equation Editor 3.0 or MathType only for equations or for formulas that cannot be produced as Word text using the Times or Symbol font.
237	
238	### Computer code
239	
240	Because altering computer code in any way (e.g., indents, line spacing, line breaks, page breaks) during the typesetting process could alter its meaning, we treat computer code differently from the rest of the article in the production process. Supply separate files for computer code.
241	
242	#### In online supplemental material
243	
244	Runnable source code should be included as supplemental material to the article. For more information, visit[supplementing your article with online material](https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/resources/supplemental-material).
245	
246	#### In the text of the article
247	
248	If authors would like to include code in the text of the published article,submit a separate file with your code exactly as it should appear, using Courier New font with a type size of 8 points. An image will be made of each segment of code in your article that exceeds 40 characters in length. (Shorter snippets of code that appear in text will be typeset in Courier New and run in with the rest of the text.)If an appendix contains a mix of code and explanatory text, please submit a file that contains the entire appendix, with the code keyed in 8-point Courier New.
249	
250	## Permissions
251	
252	Authors of accepted papers must obtain and provide to the editor on final acceptance all necessary permissions to reproduce in print and electronic form any copyrighted work, including test materials (or portions thereof), photographs, and other graphic images (including those used as stimuli in experiments).
253	
254	On advice of counsel, APA may decline to publish any image whose copyright status is unknown.
255	
256	*   [Download Permissions Alert Form (PDF, 13KB)opens in new window](https://www.apa.org/pubs/authors/permissions-alert.pdf)
257	
258	## Open science badges
259	
260	Articles are eligible for open science badges recognizing publicly available data, materials, and/or preregistered plans and analyses. These badges are awarded on a self-disclosure basis.
261	
262	At submission, authors must confirm that criteria have been fulfilled in a signed [badge disclosure form (PDF, 33KB)opens in new window](https://www.apa.org/pubs/authors/open-practices-disclosure-form.pdf) that must be submitted as supplemental material. If the editorial team confirms that all criteria have been met, the form will then be published with the article as supplemental material.
263	
264	Authors should also note their eligibility for the badge(s) in the cover letter.
265	
266	For all badges, items must be made available on an open-access repository with a persistent identifier in a format that is time-stamped, immutable, and permanent. For the preregistered badge, this is an institutional registration system.
267	
268	Data and materials must be made available under an open license allowing others to copy, share, and use the data, with attribution and copyright as applicable.
269	
270	### Available badges
271	
272	**![Image 1: Open Science badge to acknowledge Open Data research practices](https://www.apa.org/images/badge-open-data_tcm7-213184_w1024_n.png) Open Data:**  
273	All data necessary to reproduce the reported results that are digitally shareable are made publicly available. Information necessary for replication (e.g., codebooks or metadata) must be included.
274	
275	**![Image 2: Open Science badge to acknowledge Open Data: Protected Access research practices](https://www.apa.org/images/badge-open-data-protected-access_tcm7-230537_w1024_n.png) Open Data; Protected Access:**  
276	A Protected Access (PA) notation may be added to open data badges if sensitive, personal data are available only from an approved third-party repository that manages access to data to qualified researchers through a documented process. To be eligible for an open data badge with such a notation, the repository must publicly describe the steps necessary to obtain the data and detailed data documentation (e.g. variable names and allowed values) must be made available publicly. Manuscripts with data deposited in ICPSR's database are eligible for this badge.
277	
278	**![Image 3: Open Science badge to acknowledge Open Materials data practices](https://www.apa.org/images/badge-open-materials_tcm7-213185_w1024_n.png) Open Materials:**  
279	All materials necessary to reproduce the reported results that are digitally shareable, along with descriptions of non-digital materials necessary for replication, are made publicly available.
280	
281	**![Image 4: Open Science badge to acknowledge Preregistered study registration status](https://www.apa.org/images/badge-preregistered_tcm7-213186_w1024_n.png) Preregistered:**  
282	At least one study's design has been preregistered with descriptions of (a) the research design and study materials, including the planned sample size; (b) the motivating research question or hypothesis; (c) the outcome variable(s); and (d) the predictor variables, including controls, covariates, and independent variables. Results must be fully disclosed. As long as they are distinguished from other results in the article, results from analyses that were not preregistered may be reported in the article.
283	
284	**![Image 5: Open Science badge to acknowledge Preregistered+Analysis Plan study registration status](https://www.apa.org/images/badge-preregistered-plus_tcm7-213187_w1024_n.png) Preregistered+Analysis Plan:**  
285	At least one study's design has been preregistered along with an analysis plan for the research — and results are recorded according to that plan.
286	
287	Note that it may not be possible to preregister a study or to share data and materials. Applying for open science badges is optional.
288	
289	## APA publishing policies and practices
290	
291	APA holds policies that apply to all journals published. These include policies on author contributorship and responsibilities of authors; author name changes after publication; the use of generative artificial intelligence; funder information and conflict-of-interest disclosures; duplicate publication; data publication and reuse; and preprints.Please also refer to individual journal submission guidance for specific practices and requirements for manuscript submission.
292	
293	### Peer review
294	
295	A key convention in the publication of research is the peer review process, in which the quality and potential contribution of each manuscript is evaluated by one's peers in the scientific community. Like other scientific journals, APA journals utilize a peer review process to guide manuscript selection and publication decisions.
296	
297	### Prior dissemination
298	
299	In light of changing patterns of scientific knowledge dissemination, APA requires authors to provide information on prior dissemination of the data and narrative interpretations of the data/research appearing in the manuscript (e.g., if some or all were presented at a conference or meeting, posted on a listserv, shared on a website, including academic social networks like ResearchGate, etc.). This information (2–4 sentences) must be provided as part of the author note.
300	
301	### Concurrent consideration
302	
303	APA policy prohibits an author from submitting the same manuscript for concurrent consideration by two or more publications.
304	
305	### Conflicts of interest
306	
307	APA requires authors to reveal any possible conflict of interest in the conduct and reporting of research (e.g.,financial interests in a test or procedure, funding by pharmaceutical companies for drug research).
308	
309	### Equity, diversity, and inclusion in APA Journals
310	
311	APA Journals aims to address systemic inequities and bias, promote equitable opportunities for researchers, and foster an inclusive environment within the psychological research and scholarly publishing communities, representative of the wide array of people that psychology consists of and serves.Please refer to individual journal submission guidance for specific EDI practices and requirements for manuscript submission.
312	
313	### Open science
314	
315	The APA Journals™ Program is committed to publishing transparent, rigorous research; improving reproducibility in science; and aiding research discovery. Open science practices vary across subfields and per editor discretion, and APA Publishing supports all efforts to improve openness and transparency, especially as they improve diversity, equity, and inclusion.Please refer to individual journal submission guidance for specific OS practices and requirements for manuscript submission.
316	
317	### Open access
318	
319	The APA Journals Office supports authors’ choices on how to publish their work. We are committed to offering options that we believe comply with most funder and institutional requirements and support both self-archiving (“green”) and APC (paid for via an article processing charge and also known as “gold”) Open Access options.Submitting a manuscript for peer review is free of charge.
320	
321	### Generative artificial intelligence
322	
323	APA’s current policies on generative AI include:
324	
325	*   When a generative AI model is used in the drafting of a manuscript for an APA publication, the use of AI must be disclosed in the methods section and cited.
326	*   AI cannot be named as an author on an APA scholarly publication.
327	
328	### Internet posting guidelines
329	
330	APA policy prohibits an author from submitting the same manuscript for concurrent consideration by two or more publications.Preprints are allowed.
331	
332	### Permission to reproduce copyrighted work
333	
334	Authors of accepted papers must obtain and provide on final acceptance all necessary permissions to reproduce in print and electronic form any copyrighted work, including test materials (or portions thereof), photographs, and other graphic images (including those used as stimuli in experiments).
335	
336	On advice of counsel, APA may decline to publish any image whose copyright status is unknown.
337	
338	## Ethical Principles
339	
340	It is a violation of APA Ethical Principles to publish “as original data, data that have been previously published” (Standard 8.13).
341	
342	APA Ethical Principles also state that “after research results are published, psychologists do not withhold the data on which their conclusions are based from other competent professionals who seek to verify the substantive claims through reanalysis and who intend to use such data only for that purpose, provided that the confidentiality of the participants can be protected and unless legal rights concerning proprietary data preclude their release” (Standard 8.14).
343	
344	APA expects authors to make their data available if asked during the editorial process and for at least five years after the date of publication.
345	
346	If the manuscript is accepted, the corresponding author is required to sign and submit a [Certification of Compliance with APA Ethical Principles (PDF, 26KB).opens in new window](https://www.apa.org/pubs/authors/ethics.pdf)
347	
348	## Other information
349	
350	See [APA’s Publishing Policies page](https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/resources/publishing-policies) for more information on publication policies, including information on author contributorship and responsibilities of authors, author name changes after publication, the use of generative artificial intelligence, funder information and conflict-of-interest disclosures, duplicate publication, data publication and reuse, and preprints.
351	
352	Visit the [Journals Publishing Resource Center](https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/resources) for more resources for writing, reviewing, and editing articles for publishing in APA journals.
353

Markdown Content:
Generative artificial intelligence, specifically the kind based on Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, has become a transformative force in many fields. Scholarly writing and publishing are no different, and generative AI has begun to have an impact on scholarly work.

In response to this impact, the APA Publications and Communications Board has approved policies regarding the use of generative AI in scholarly materials. These policies (as well as APA policies on other potential issues in scholarly publishing, and additional reading on the subject) can be found on the [APA Publishing Policies page](https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/resources/publishing-policies)and will continue to develop as we gain a better understanding of the effects of generative AI on scholarly publishing.

APA’s current policies on generative AI are:

*   When a generative AI model is used in the drafting of a manuscript for an APA publication, the use of AI must be disclosed in the methods section and cited.
*   AI cannot be named as an author on an APA scholarly publication.

## Authors

APA policy states that authors are responsible for the accuracy of any information in their article. This means that authors must verify any information and citations provided to them by an AI tool. Authors may use, but must disclose, AI tools for specific purposes such as editing.

For guidance about when and where to disclose the use of a Generative AI tool, please see the [disclosure guidance](https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/resources/publishing-tips/policy-generative-ai#disclosure-guidance) section below.

Additionally, please note that when information is entered into generative AI, the organization which runs the generative AI will likely have access to this data. Authors should be aware of this possibility and how it may impact the privacy of participants in their studies, as well as how it may impact their own privacy and intellectual property. For this reason, journal editors and reviewers may not enter materials from submitted manuscripts into generative AI as it would constitute a violation of the confidentiality of the peer review process.

## Disclosure guidance

Guiding principles for authors and editors about what output to disclose from generative AI tools:

*   Authors need to **be transparent**, providing the necessary information for readers to understand how generative artificial intelligence (AI) was used during the research and manuscript drafting process. Disclose the use in the most relevant place in the manuscript, most likely the Introduction or Method sections.
*   Authors need to **maintain ethical approaches** to using generative AI, including not entering confidential material into open generative AI tools, for example, research data or client notes that may make a participant/client identifiable.
*   Authors need to **take responsibility** for the information provided by generative AI tools, including verifying the information received via generative AI searches by reading original sources used in AI output.
*   Authors need to **provide attribution** to the generative AI tool in cases where the tool was used to generate ideas, content, analysis, code, or research elements. If you would provide attribution to a human contributor, you should most likely provide attribution to a generative AI tool for a similar activity.

Authors should consider the disclosure of AI in the context of existing resources such as the _Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association_ (7th ed.), the _Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct_, the Contributor Role Taxonomy (

[CRediT opens in new window](https://credit.niso.org/)
), and guidance provided by the institution that approved the author’s research. For curated AI topics, consult the [APA Style website and blog](https://apastyle.apa.org/search?query=AI).

Noncomprehensive examples of these principles are provided next to aid authors and editors in thinking about what needs to be disclosed when using generative AI. Some examples recommend that authors preserve the output of generative AI in their private records in case it is requested during peer review or after publication. Researchers should document for their own records the prompts used with AI tools. To the extent that it helps readers, these prompts can be included where the AI use is disclosed, or elsewhere as appropriate, such as an appendix.

Guidance on what to disclose and where in manuscripts or coursework*

| Generative AI use | How to disclose | Similar principle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Generate a resource list on a topic to inform your literature review, metasynthesis, meta-analysis, or similar | In the introduction section, including your prompts, keywords, and AI used. (Preserve the output in case of inquiry) | Listing databases queried with what keywords and filters were used when describing literature search strategy for a literature review, metasynthesis, or meta-analysis |
| Translate text included in the manuscript or implement extensive copyediting (more than you’d traditionally find in Microsoft Word and similar tools) | In a general note in the author note, including the tool used | Similar to the _Writing – Review and Editing_ CRediT role, only generative AI may not be listed as an author |
| Create or refine code | In the Method section, including the tool used and number of iterations (preserve the output in case of inquiry) | Describing the statistical package used in analysis, such as R or SPSS |
| Analyze, refine, format, or visualize data | In the Method section, including the tool used and number of iterations (preserve the output in case of inquiry) | Describing the statistical package and visualization tools used in analysis, such as R or SPSS |
| Write or draft manuscript content, including literature summaries and outlines | In the introduction section, including your prompts and tool used |  |
| Create or edit figures, tables, and/or images | In the section where the figures, tables, and/or images appear (e.g., Results section), including your prompts and tool used (preserve the output in case of inquiry) |  |
| Create or edit research design elements, data, or results | In the Method section (preserve the output in case of inquiry) |  |

*Authors should consider this as guidance only and defer to the requirements of the journal editor as relevant.

# Jisc Member Institutions
Authors affiliated with UK institutions participating in APA’s Jisc agreement may publish open access in hybrid journals published by APA at no cost to the author, provided that:
*   The article’s corresponding author is affiliated with a participating institution's UK campus.
*   The article is accepted after August 1, 2022.
*   The article is an original peer-reviewed research article or review article.
All articles under this agreement will be published under the CC-BY copyright license. Upon publication, articles will be made immediately open access.
[Read the press release](https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2022/08/jisc-open-access-publishing) for more information on the open access agreement.
expand all
How to submit an article for consideration
Authors who meet the above requirements can submit their manuscript via the submission portal of the selected journal. Upon submission, the corresponding author must provide funder information and a Ringgold affiliation ID. If the submission is accepted, the author will be ushered through an open access and copyright approval process.
APA Journals is using CCC’s RightsLink as our open access articles processing platform. General resources for navigating RightsLink can be found in the [Author Resource Center opens in new window](https://www.copyright.com/rlauthorrc/), and as a [training video opens in new window](https://player.vimeo.com/video/920647936?dnt=1&badge=0&autopause=0&player_id=0&app_id=58479) that details our APA-spe
As of August 2023, articles in journals published by Hogrefe that are part of the PsycArticles database are also included under Jisc’s agreement. Further information on the [submission process for Hogrefe journals opens in new window](https://www.hogrefe.com/eu/service/for-journal-authors/openmind/oa-psycarticles) can be found online.
Is there a limit on open access articles published as part of this agreement?
Yes, APA and Jisc have set a limit on the maximum number of open access articles to be published for each year of this partnership. If the maximum number is reached, institutions will work with authors on alternative options for their articles.

163:The use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT or Large Language Models in research publications is expanding rapidly. COPE joins organisations, such as WAME and the JAMA Network among others, to state that AI tools cannot be listed as an author of a paper.
164:AI tools cannot meet the requirements for authorship as they cannot take responsibility for the submitted work. As non-legal entities, they cannot assert the presence or absence of conflicts of interest nor manage copyright and license agreements.
165:Authors who use AI tools in the writing of a manuscript, production of images or graphical elements of the paper, or in the collection and analysis of data, must be transparent in disclosing in the Materials and Methods (or similar section) of the paper how the AI tool was used and which tool was used. Authors are fully responsible for the content of their manuscript, even those parts produced by an AI tool, and are thus liable for any breach of publication ethics.

## about
# Journal information
_Decision_ is a multidisciplinary journal focused on scientific research into human judgment and decision-making. This includes research on neural, cognitive, social, economic, cultural, and environmental aspects of people’s decisions.
_Decision_ publishes articles on all areas related to the psychology of judgment and decision-making including probabilistic inference, prediction, evaluation, choice, decisions under risk or uncertainty, and economic games. The journal publishes articles reporting new empirical research that adds to our understanding of judgment and decision making, and articles that present and evaluate new theory.
To achieve this goal, _Decision_ publishes three types of articles: long articles that make major theoretical contributions, shorter articles that make valuable empirical contributions addressing important research questions, and brief review articles that target current theoretical trends or new topics in decision making. Title: Tim Rakow, PhD
URL Source: https://www.apa.org/pubs/highlights/editor-spotlight/dec-rakow
Markdown Content:
![Image 1: Editor Spotlight: Tim Rakow, PhD](https://www.apa.org/images/index-editor-spotlight-dec-rakow_tcm7-327849_w1024_n.jpg) Rakow is a reader (associate professor) in psychology at King’s College London, where he researches judgment and decision making and is deputy director for a large undergraduate psychology programme.
## Background
**Tell us a bit about your background: What is your area of research? What is your most recent journal-editing experience?**
In my research, I investigate a range of topics from the field of judgment and decision making (JDM). My main paradigm for this research is experimental cognitive psychology, which has informed my lab studies of probabilistic inference, decisions from experience, deliberative thinking, valuation, and choice under risk and uncertainty. I also have a more applied line of research that examines clinical judgment and risk communication in medicine and health. As with my basic research studies, in this contextualized research I typically use experimental designs.
I was an associate editor at _Thinking & Reasoning_ (2012–2023), where I handled the JDM submissions. In that role, I aimed to provide authors with as much constructive feedback as possible. I have also adopted this as a goal for my editorship at _Decision_.
## Journal importance
**Why is this journal important for the field?**
JDM research is truly interdisciplinary. It profitably draws on insights from economics, cognitive science, philosophy, and statistical theory, to name but a few fields. However, to my mind, it is important to have a JDM journal that is sponsored by one of psychology’s prominent academic societies. Psychologists have made major contributions to the understanding of people’s judgments and decisions, and these contributions have come from diverse fields of study within psychology—biological, cognitive, social, developmental, and mathematical psychology—as well as from psychology’s applied research areas. And this works both ways. Because decision making is a core behavior, the findings and conclusions from JDM research are valuable for researchers working in different areas of psychology. Given these connections and overlaps between decision research and multiple areas of psychology resear
## Plans
**Have you introduced or are you planning to introduce any changes?**
I have added two manuscript types to those that will be considered for publication in _Decision_.
First, _Decision_ now invites submissions of _registered replication report_ s. Such manuscripts offer the opportunity for conditional acceptance before data are collected if authors can demonstrate the value of conducting replication research and have a solid plan for conducting that research to a high standard. Acceptance of the final version depends only on following the agreed plan, irrespective of what the data show. The benefits of this format have been widely discussed, and _Decision_ is one of several journals to have begun inviting submissions of this type in recent years.
The second new manuscript type is the _registered adversarial collaboration_. This format has several similarities to the registered replication report but is likely something that readers and authors are less familiar with. In an adversarial collaboration, researchers (or research teams) with opposing positions on a research question or theoretical issue commit to an agreed plan for empirical research that offers a realistic opportunity for some adjudication or resolution vis-à-vis their respective positions. Much like with a registered replication report, the conditional acceptance of a registered adversarial collaboration depends only on the case that the authors make for their research and the quality and feasibility of their collaborative research plan. Such collaborations are relatively rare, but the lesson learned from those that have been published is that they promote high-quali
The [journal’s webpage](https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/dec) has guidance for preparing and submitting manuscripts of either of these new types, each of which has been embedded in the journal’s systems for peer review.
## Priorities
**What type of scholarship would you like to see in the journal, and what kind of content are you hoping to attract?**
I would like to see good scholarship and good content! To expand on that, I am aware that the wording of an invitation to submit research to a journal may leave researchers in doubt over whether their scholarship is welcome. Many labels are used to describe research of different types, such as “basic,” “applied,” or “translational” research, or the focus or contribution of an article, such as “theoretical” or “empirical.” Although I, like others, find these labels convenient and useful, I have become increasingly mindful that the distinctions they imply are not clear-cut. _Applied_ and _translational_ research can provide insights into _basic_ decision processes. Well-designed _empirical_ investigations can test _theory_ even though the researchers’ write-up may focus on establishing the reliability of the phenomenon rather than the mechanism that generates it. In light of this, I want t
As a final answer to this question, I can suggest a strategy for identifying suitable topics for registered replication reports, which is loosely inspired by the findings of Christensen-Szalanski and Beach (1984), a published comment that I think I first read as a PhD student. In the 1970s, Jay J. J. Christensen-Szalanski and Lee Roy Beach surveyed JDM researchers and found that their impressions about the general quality of human judgment seemed to be based on a restricted range of prominent research studies. Now, I am not one of those doomsayers who believes that psychology has few replicable findings, but I do worry that a handful of JDM’s “textbook examples” have not had the degree of scrutiny that a classic finding deserves. For example, unlike most other go-to examples, my classroom demonstrations have never successfully reproduced the intransitive choice preferences that Tversky (
Date created: May 2024

[![Image 2: Cover of Decision (small)](https://www.apa.org/images/dec-100_tcm7-147252_w1024_n.gif)](https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/dec)
[_Decision_](https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/dec) is a multidisciplinary research journal focused on a theoretical understanding of neural, cognitive, social, and economic aspects of human judgment and decision-making behavior. Decision publishes articles on all areas related to judgment and decision-making research including probabilistic inference, prediction, evaluation, choice, decisions under risk or uncertainty, and economic games.
